Our toll-free number is 1-800-458-3525 or you can send an email to holotalk at holoworld.com. We've got telephone calls, we've got emails, we've got special guests coming up. And by the area I mean if you live in the New York, Philadelphia, Baltimore, Washington, D.C. corridor and take that west over to Harrisburg and make a rectangle out of that. If you're somewhere in that area, this holography exhibit is going to be a very easy trip for you to go to and see. And this is going to be a major exhibit for lasers and holograms. The book calls for a light reading before I shoot it. I got a little confused about the light reading because there are two beams hitting the object. Do I take the reading as I would on a single-beam reflection, concentrating on the reference beam and ignoring the object beam? Well, you wouldn't have two beams if you were doing a single-beam reflection, but I know what you mean there. Or is there another way to do it? No, go in there and take readings of both your object and reference beam, and the way you do the reference beam is typical. You just take your probe and point it down towards the lens or whatever you're using, the angle that that reference beam is coming in, and move it around the plate area. You can hold it right in the plane of the plate holder. Move it around and get an average reading. You know, you're going to have a hotspot probably right in the middle if you don't have the beam spread out that much, but you want to spread that beam out enough that you're not going to see that much of a variation from the center of where your hologram is going to be recorded out to the edges. So you try and spread that area out as much as possible. You do lose a lot of power. And if you don't have a lot of power to spare, then you don't want to spread that beam out too much, but you want to try and avoid that hotspot in the middle. You're going to need your object out of place to do this, because you've got to get your hand right down in there and hold that probe in the plane of the plate holder. Now for the object beam, you just put your object back in there, take the probe, go around the other side, point it toward the object right in the plane of where your film or your plate is going to be, and just go around that object and get a number of different readings. You don't absolutely have to have a 90-10 beam splitter. I've never had a variable beam splitter. I just never spent the money for it. I have a selection of little beam splitters about the size of microscope slides. Some of them are 90-10, 75-25, 60-40, 50-50. And I will use whatever beam splitter I need. What's going to determine that is the fact of how bright or how much light your object is going to reflect. We can tell you what's going wrong. It's a shame you've done eight and you're still getting that. But from what you've explained right here in the email, I can't really tell what it is that could be the problem. So if you want to email me again, let me know if there's some way I can take a look at it, or if you want to put it up on the web, a bunch of us that are involved with holography can take a look. And we can get back to you as far as what we think would be good corrective measures for that hologram. Okay, we have someone that's writing that's confused in England. And this guy's name is, well, I can't say it's a guy. It's Chris. I guess it could be a young lady as well. Chris writes, is it true that when a hologram shatters, the whole image can be seen in all the broken parts? If so, why does this happen? Well, this is something a lot of people always talk about, the fact that you can take a hologram, break it up into a thousand pieces, and each one of the pieces contain the entire holographic image. That's true to a point. We've had this question a number of other times on the show. And what actually happens is you can see the image. This happens best with a laser transmission hologram, because laser transmission holograms are made, and usually, more than likely, the object is quite a bit of distance from the holographic plate, compared to a reflection hologram, where you have the object as close to the plate as possible. When that object is located quite a bit of distance from the plate, and you break that plate up, you can still see the whole object, but you see it through the perspective of wherever that piece of glass came from. And if you picked up the lower right-hand corner, and looked through that piece of glass, you'd still see the whole object, but you'd see it from the perspective of the lower right corner. If anyone out there offers courses, please email me and I'll be happy to put you on a list so people can get in touch with you as well. Royal College of Art in London, I believe, also has a degree program in holography. But physics would be the strong point, I would imagine, if you wanted to get involved with holography. But I'm not quite sure how it's approached from the art end. I know there are a number of different artists who are involved with holography, and I'm not quite sure how they would approach it. I think it's important to know that there are a number of different artists who are involved with holography, and a lot of them don't approach it from the science and technology standpoint as much as they approach it from the creative standpoint of an artist. So it depends on what you would want to get out of holography in the end concerning what it is you should, or how you should approach holography as part of your studies. If you have any, I would appreciate any help you could give me. Thanks a lot. I appreciate it. Once the holograms are made, I can't really think of too many things of doing a science fair project with them. You could do a number of different experiments. Of course, you could get holograms and illuminate them with different lights and find out what the result would be from different lights illuminating the holograms.

number of different experiments. Of course, you could get holograms and illuminate them with different lights and find out what the result would be from different lights illuminating the hologram. And you could compare that with reflection holograms and white light transmission holograms. Even embossed holograms would probably be easiest for you. But outside of actually making holograms, just offhand, I can't think of very many science fair projects you could do with already made holograms. You have a much better choice going with lasers and doing a science fair project working with lasers. All right, so that just about catches us up with our email questions. We're going to have area students involved with it, and we'll be doing that live here as well. Just send an email to me at holotalk at holoworld.com, and just mark in that email. I'd like to come out and see the show being done. So I'll send an email back and give you some more information on that. So thank you very much for tuning in. This is Frankie Freitas for Holotalk, and we'll see you next week.
